Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The investigation of the E. coli outbreak linked to Nestle Toll House cookie dough is nearly over, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The cause of the contamination has not been identified. Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. David Acheson, the FDA's associate commissioner for foods, says the samples of cookie dough his agency has tested do not contain the E. coli strain that sickened 74 people in 32 states. On June 19, Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. Thirty-four people have been hospitalized; no deaths have been reported. The CDC reports that the majority of the patients were teenage girls who reported eating the cookie dough raw. Last month, the FDA found E. coli in a production sample of Toll House cookie dough, but after testing, investigators found that the strain in the sample did not match the outbreak strain. "We are still in speculation mode," Acheson said, but the E. coli "most likely came from raw ingredients" such as flour. The E.coli strain that caused the outbreak, 0157:H7, is typically found in fecal contamination from animals such as cows, sheep or goats. Acheson points out that it's not unusual for those animals to be carrying more than one strain of the bacteria. But he believes that the root cause of the contamination may never be known. "We have to conclude we're unlikely to have a definitive determination," he said. Most people with E. coli 0157:H7 experience diarrhea and abdominal cramps within eight days of infection. The FDA notified Nestle USA on Thursday that its investigation at the Danville plant was over. Nestle says FDA inspectors were at the plant for more than a week and found no E. coli on equipment. More than 1,000 tests have been conducted at the facility after the outbreak. "We've dismantled the production line and done extensive testing on all equipment and not found any E. coli," Nestle USA spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald said. MacDonald announced that Nestle is easing back into production at the plant. The company has purchased new lots of eggs, flour and margarine and says it is thoroughly testing the new products and all raw ingredients. Consumers will have to wait to see cookie dough back in grocery stores. "You're not going to see anything on the shelves for quite some time," MacDonald said. But when it does appear, the company will mark the cookie dough with a new label that clearly designates it as a new batch. It will also continue to carry a reminder to not eat the dough raw.

# FDA Nears Conclusion in Toll House Cookie Dough E. Coli Investigation Without Pinpointing Source

The Food and Drug Administration's investigation into an E. coli outbreak linked to Nestle Toll House refrigerated cookie dough is drawing to a close, though officials acknowledge they have been unable to definitively identify the exact source of contamination. Despite months of rigorous testing and analysis, the precise origin of the bacteria that sickened dozens of consumers across the country remains a mystery.

The outbreak prompted Nestle to issue a sweeping recall of all Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products manufactured at its Danville, Virginia facility. The company took this action after health officials confirmed that 74 people across 32 states had fallen ill after consuming the product. Of those affected, 34 required hospitalization, though fortunately no deaths were reported in connection with the outbreak.

In examining the pattern of illness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention uncovered a notable trend among those affected: the majority of patients were teenage girls who admitted to eating the cookie dough raw, straight from the package, rather than baking it as intended. This behavior, while common among consumers of the popular product, significantly increased their risk of exposure to the harmful bacteria, since raw dough is not subjected to the heat treatment that would typically kill such pathogens during baking.

FDA officials have developed a working theory that points to raw ingredients—particularly flour—as the most probable source of the E. coli contamination. This hypothesis is significant because flour is not typically treated to eliminate bacteria in the same way other food products might be, making it a plausible vector for contamination that could easily go undetected until finished products reach consumers. However, this remains a theory rather than a confirmed finding, as investigators were unable to locate concrete evidence to support it.

Extensive testing conducted at the Danville manufacturing plant failed to reveal any contamination on equipment or surfaces used in production. In total, investigators carried out more than 1,000 separate tests throughout the facility, examining various potential contamination points, yet none of these tests yielded positive results that could conclusively link the outbreak to a specific piece of equipment, process, or location within the plant.

Given these inconclusive results despite such a comprehensive investigative effort, David Acheson, the FDA's associate commissioner for foods, has candidly stated that a definitive determination of the outbreak's root cause may never be established. This admission underscores the inherent challenges in tracing foodborne illness outbreaks to their exact source, particularly when the contamination may have occurred at an earlier stage in the supply chain—such as during the growing, harvesting, or processing of raw ingredients—before products ever reached the manufacturing facility where the final testing took place.

The Food and Drug Administration announced that its extensive investigation into an E. coli outbreak linked to prepackaged Nestle Toll House cookie dough is drawing to a close, though the exact source of contamination may never be conclusively determined. The outbreak, which began earlier this year, sickened at least 74 people across 32 states and resulted in 34 hospitalizations. Notably, the majority of those affected were teenage girls, many of whom admitted to consuming the cookie dough raw rather than baking it first—a practice health officials have long warned against due to the risks posed by raw eggs and untreated flour.

Despite this thorough and time-consuming process, none of the samples collected from the plant's equipment tested positive for E. coli, and critically, none of the strains identified in any samples matched the particular strain responsible for the outbreak.

This lack of a definitive match has led officials to conclude that pinpointing the precise origin of the contamination may not be possible. Investigators have pointed to raw ingredients—particularly flour—as a likely suspect, since flour is not treated to kill pathogens the way many other food ingredients are and has been implicated in previous foodborne illness outbreaks. However, without direct evidence linking a specific ingredient or point in the production process to the outbreak strain, the FDA acknowledges that the mystery may remain unsolved.

The case has renewed public health warnings about the dangers of consuming raw cookie dough and other uncooked baked goods, as both raw eggs and flour can harbor harmful bacteria that are only neutralized through proper baking or cooking. # FDA Closes Investigation Into Nestlé Toll House Cookie Dough E. Coli Outbreak

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has officially closed its investigation into the E. coli contamination linked to prepackaged Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough, an outbreak that sickened dozens of consumers across the United States.

The outbreak, which prompted a nationwide recall, was traced back to a Nestlé USA manufacturing facility located in Danville, Virginia. According to health officials, the contamination resulted in at least 72 reported illnesses across more than 30 states, with a significant number of those affected requiring hospitalization due to complications from the E. coli O157:H7 strain.

Nestlé voluntarily recalled all varieties of its prepackaged cookie dough products in the wake of the outbreak, urging consumers not to consume the raw dough and to discard or return any purchased products. The company cooperated with both the FDA and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) throughout the investigation, which included extensive testing at the Danville facility and product sampling from affected households.

Despite the widespread illnesses, investigators were unable to pinpoint a definitive single source of contamination within the plant, though officials noted that flour used in the dough recipe was considered a possible contributing factor—an ingredient not typically associated with E. coli risk in products intended to be baked before consumption.

In closing the investigation, the FDA stated that corrective actions taken by Nestlé at the Danville facility, including enhanced sanitation protocols and supply chain testing measures, were sufficient to address the immediate public health concern. The agency emphasized that no new cases linked to the affected products have been reported in recent months.

Nestlé has since reformulated its cookie dough products, adding heat-treated flour and pasteurized eggs to reduce the risk of bacterial contamination, and has updated packaging to include more prominent warnings against consuming raw dough.

Consumer advocacy groups have welcomed the closure of the case but continue to push for stricter industry-wide standards regarding raw dough products, citing the persistent risk posed by uncooked flour and eggs in similar consumer goods.

The FDA noted that while this particular investigation has concluded, it will continue to monitor food safety practices at facilities producing ready-to-eat and raw dough products nationwide.

# FDA Investigation Concludes Without Definitive Source for Cookie Dough E. Coli Outbreak

**Federal officials say root cause of contamination may remain unknown despite extensive investigation**

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has indicated that investigators may never pinpoint the exact source of E. coli contamination linked to raw, prepackaged cookie dough, despite months of testing, facility inspections, and supply chain analysis.

## Why the Trail Went Cold

Health officials cite several factors complicating the investigation:

- **Perishable evidence**: By the time illnesses were reported and traced back to specific product batches, the contaminated ingredients or production runs had often already been consumed, discarded, or were no longer available for testing.

- **Complex supply chains**: Cookie dough products typically contain multiple ingredients—flour, eggs, and other components—sourced from numerous suppliers. E. coli could theoretically have entered at any point in this chain, from farm to processing facility to distribution.

- **Flour as a suspect**: Investigators have increasingly focused on raw flour as a potential vehicle for contamination, since flour is not a "ready-to-eat" product and doesn't undergo a kill-step (like baking) before packaging for raw dough consumption. However, confirming flour as the definitive source has proven difficult.

- **Time lag in reporting**: E. coli symptoms can take days to appear, and consumers may not immediately connect illness to cookie dough consumption, further delaying sample collection from the original contaminated product.

## Nestlé's Response

In response to the outbreak and ongoing uncertainty, Nestlé USA has emphasized its cooperation with federal investigators while implementing precautionary measures:

- **Voluntary recall**: The company voluntarily recalled affected cookie dough products as a precautionary measure, even without full confirmation of the contamination source.

- **Enhanced testing protocols**: Nestlé has stated it is increasing pathogen testing across its supply chain, including more rigorous screening of raw ingredients like flour and eggs.

- **Consumer messaging**: The company has reinforced labeling and public messaging warning that raw cookie dough is not intended for consumption before baking, regardless of "safe to eat raw" marketing some products have carried in the past.

- **Supplier audits**: Nestlé says it is conducting additional audits of ingredient suppliers to identify and mitigate potential contamination risks further up the supply chain.

## Broader Food Safety Implications

This case highlights a persistent challenge in food safety investigations: contamination in complex, multi-ingredient products can be difficult to trace with certainty, even when the outbreak itself is clearly linked to a specific product category.

Food safety experts note that such cases often result in improved industry-wide practices—such as heat-treating flour or advising against consuming raw dough—even when a singular contamination point is never definitively identified.

The FDA continues to recommend that consumers avoid eating raw cookie dough and follow package instructions to bake products thoroughly before consumption.
